claim: Genome packaging in large double-stranded DNA viruses requires a powerful molecular motor to force the viral genome into nascent capsids.
source: Genome packaging in large double-stranded DNA viruses requires a powerful molecular motor to force the viral genome into nascent capsids, which involves essential accessory factors that are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a general statement about viral genome packaging that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: ORF68 and BFLF1 form homopentameric rings with a positively charged central channel that binds double-stranded DNA.
source: These homologous proteins form highly similar homopentameric rings with a positively charged central channel that binds double-stranded DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM and crystallography, as well as biochemical binding assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mutation of individual positively charged residues within the central channel ablates DNA binding.
source: Mutation of individual positively charged residues within but not outside the channel ablates DNA binding, and in the context of KSHV infection, these mutants fail to package the viral genome or produce progeny virions.
evidence: This is supported by electrophoretic mobility shift assays showing loss of DNA binding for channel mutants.

claim: ORF68 mutants with mutations in the central channel fail to package the viral genome or produce progeny virions in KSHV infection.
source: Mutation of individual positively charged residues within but not outside the channel ablates DNA binding, and in the context of KSHV infection, these mutants fail to package the viral genome or produce progeny virions.
evidence: This is supported by supernatant transfer assays and Southern blot analyses showing packaging defects.

claim: Nearly all adults in the world harbor at least one of the nine human herpesviruses.
source: The ability of herpesviruses to efficiently evade the immune system and establish latency, coupled with few available treatments and vaccines, means that nearly all adults in the world harbor at least one of the nine human herpesviruses.
evidence: This is a statement based on established epidemiological knowledge about herpesvirus prevalence.

claim: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) is an alphaherpesvirus that causes cold sores and genital sores.
source: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) is an alphaherpesvirus that causes cold sores and genital sores.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSV-1 classification and disease manifestations.

claim: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a betaherpesvirus that can cause mononucleosis and congenital birth defects.
source: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a betaherpesvirus that can cause mononucleosis and congenital birth defects.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HCMV classification and disease manifestations.

claim: KSHV and EBV are oncogenic viruses that cause cancers such as primary effusion lymphoma and Kaposi's sarcoma.
source: The human gamma-herpesviruses Kaposi's sarcoma-associated virus (KSHV) and Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) are oncogenic viruses, causing cancers such as primary effusion lymphoma and Kaposi's sarcoma (in the case of KSHV).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the oncogenic properties of these gammaherpesviruses.

claim: 400 million years of evolution separate the human herpesviruses.
source: Despite 400 million years of evolution separating the human herpesviruses, several core pathways in replication are conserved (McGeoch et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McGeoch et al., 2006.

claim: Several core pathways in replication are conserved across human herpesviruses.
source: Despite 400 million years of evolution separating the human herpesviruses, several core pathways in replication are conserved (McGeoch et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McGeoch et al., 2006.

claim: Herpesviruses replicate their genome as a head-to-tail concatemer of linked genomes separated by terminal repeats near the end of the lytic cycle.
source: Near the end of the lytic cycle, herpesviruses replicate their genome as a head-to-tail concatemer of linked genomes separated by terminal repeats.
evidence: This is established knowledge about herpesvirus DNA replication.

claim: Cleavage to produce a unit-length genome is intimately tied to packaging and occurs only after that genome is successfully transferred into a capsid.
source: Cleavage to produce a unit-length genome is intimately tied to packaging and occurs only after that genome is successfully transferred into a capsid.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the coupling of cleavage and packaging in herpesviruses.

claim: DNA packaging in tailed bacteriophages is thought to be mechanistically similar to that of herpesviruses.
source: DNA packaging in tailed bacteriophages is thought to be mechanistically similar to that of herpesviruses (Rixon and Schmid, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rixon and Schmid, 2014.

claim: Both bacteriophages and herpesviruses use an icosahedral capsid and an architecturally similar portal protein through which DNA is packaged.
source: Despite infecting hosts in different kingdoms, both groups of viruses use an icosahedral capsid and an architecturally similar portal protein through which DNA is packaged (Rixon and Schmid, 2014; Dedeo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rixon and Schmid, 2014 and Dedeo et al., 2019.

claim: Both bacteriophages and herpesviruses depend on a 'terminase' motor responsible for packaging and cleavage of the genome.
source: Furthermore, both depend on a 'terminase' motor responsible for packaging and cleavage of the genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about viral DNA packaging machinery.

claim: The large subunit of the terminase is the most conserved gene across the herpesviruses.
source: The large subunit of the terminase is the most conserved gene across the herpesviruses and possesses sequence and structural similarity to phage terminases, supporting the hypothesis that packaging occurs through an evolutionarily ancient mechanism (Rixon and Schmid, 2014; Nadal et al., 2010; Selvarajan Sigamani et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rixon and Schmid, 2014; Nadal et al., 2010; and Selvarajan Sigamani et al., 2013.

claim: The large subunit of the terminase possesses sequence and structural similarity to phage terminases.
source: The large subunit of the terminase is the most conserved gene across the herpesviruses and possesses sequence and structural similarity to phage terminases, supporting the hypothesis that packaging occurs through an evolutionarily ancient mechanism (Rixon and Schmid, 2014; Nadal et al., 2010; Selvarajan Sigamani et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rixon and Schmid, 2014; Nadal et al., 2010; and Selvarajan Sigamani et al., 2013.

claim: Cleavage and packaging in HSV-1 requires six conserved proteins in addition to the nascent capsid and concatemeric genome: UL6, UL15, UL17, UL28, UL32, and UL33.
source: Cleavage and packaging in the herpesviruses, best studied in HSV-1, requires six conserved proteins in addition to the nascent capsid and concatemeric genome (Heming et al., 2017): HSV-1 UL6, UL15, UL17, UL28, UL32, and UL33.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heming et al., 2017.

claim: UL15, UL28, and UL33 form the terminase motor.
source: Three of these proteins (UL15/UL28/UL33) form the terminase motor, and the portal protein is composed of a dodecamer of UL6 (Newcomb et al., 2001; Patel et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Newcomb et al., 2001 and Patel et al., 1996.

claim: The portal protein is composed of a dodecamer of UL6.
source: Three of these proteins (UL15/UL28/UL33) form the terminase motor, and the portal protein is composed of a dodecamer of UL6 (Newcomb et al., 2001; Patel et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Newcomb et al., 2001 and Patel et al., 1996.

claim: UL17 encodes a capsid vertex-specific protein important for stabilizing the capsid.
source: UL17 encodes a capsid vertex-specific protein important for stabilizing the capsid (Gong et al., 2019; Grzesik et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2019; Grzesik et al., 2017; and Liu et al., 2019.

claim: UL32 and its homologs in HCMV (UL52) and KSHV (ORF68) are essential for production of packaged virions.
source: In contrast, despite observations that UL32 and its homologs in HCMV (UL52) and KSHV (ORF68) are essential for production of packaged virions, their function in packaging remains unknown (Albright et al., 2015; Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018; Lamberti and Weller, 1998; Borst et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Albright et al., 2015; Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018; Lamberti and Weller, 1998; and Borst et al., 2008.

claim: The function of UL32 and its homologs in packaging remains unknown.
source: In contrast, despite observations that UL32 and its homologs in HCMV (UL52) and KSHV (ORF68) are essential for production of packaged virions, their function in packaging remains unknown (Albright et al., 2015; Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018; Lamberti and Weller, 1998; Borst et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is made in the context of prior literature, though the manuscript aims to address this gap.

claim: Phages lack an identifiable homolog of UL32 or ORF68.
source: Phages lack an identifiable homolog of UL32 or ORF68, suggesting that an additional level of complexity exists in herpesvirus packaging.
evidence: This is based on sequence homology searches and comparative analysis.

claim: The absence of UL32/ORF68 homologs in phages suggests that an additional level of complexity exists in herpesvirus packaging.
source: Phages lack an identifiable homolog of UL32 or ORF68, suggesting that an additional level of complexity exists in herpesvirus packaging.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of homologs in phages.

claim: ORF68 adopts a novel fold.
source: A DALI search (Holm and Rosenström, 2010) identified proteins that are similarly α-helical in nature, but none with globally similar structures, suggesting that ORF68 adopts a novel fold.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison using DALI search.

claim: ORF68 forms a homopentameric ring with a diameter of ~120 Å.
source: ORF68 forms a homopentameric ring with a diameter of ~120 Å (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by structural data from X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM, as shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Each ORF68 monomer contains three zinc fingers and several bundles of α-helices connected by loops.
source: Each monomer contains three zinc fingers and several bundles of α-helices connected by loops.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure of ORF68.

claim: The central channel of ORF68 is constricted toward the top of the ring, with a width of ~25 Å, and widens to ~45 Å at the bottom.
source: The central channel is constricted toward the top of the ring, with a width of ~25 Å, and widens to ~45 Å at the bottom (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is based on measurements from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Residues 435–451 of ORF68 form an α-helix that is anchored by H452, which coordinates a Zn ion at the bottom of the ring.
source: Residues 435–451 form an α-helix that is anchored by H452, which coordinates a Zn ion at the bottom of the ring (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Residues 167–188 of ORF68 are largely disordered, despite being anchored by C191 and C192 that participate in coordination of a Zn ion.
source: Interestingly, residues 167–188 are largely disordered, despite being anchored by C191 and C192 that participate in coordination of the same Zn ion.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure and cryo-EM maps.

claim: ORF68 is stable as a pentamer even at high concentrations of monovalent salt.
source: ORF68 is stable as a pentamer even at high concentrations of monovalent salt (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The subunit interface of ORF68 includes ~1200 Å2 of buried surface area.
source: The subunit interface includes ~1200 Å2 of buried surface area, consisting largely of van der Waals contacts and a stacking interaction between F59 of one subunit and F335 of the adjacent subunit.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The penultimate residue of ORF68, Y466, is perfectly conserved in all homologs.
source: The penultimate residue, Y466, is perfectly conserved in all homologs and located in the pentamer structure near the highly conserved residues H364 and C369 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 5a).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and structural analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Addition of a C-terminal tag to ORF68 reduces protein levels and prevents infectious virion production.
source: We found that addition of a C-terminal tag reduces protein levels and prevents infectious virion production (Figure 1—figure supplement 5c–g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5c–g.

claim: C-terminal tagging of UL52 (the ORF68 homolog in HCMV) prevented virion production and led to an aberrantly disperse localization throughout the cell.
source: This effect was also observed in HCMV, where C-terminal tagging of the ORF68 homolog, UL52, prevented virion production and led to an aberrantly disperse localization throughout the cell (Borst et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Borst et al., 2008.

claim: Disrupting the coordination of ORF68's C-terminus at the subunit interface through addition of a tag likely interferes with pentamer formation, destabilizes the protein, and prevents its function in DNA packaging and cleavage.
source: Thus, disrupting the coordination of ORF68's C-terminus at the subunit interface through addition of a tag likely interferes with pentamer formation, destabilizes the protein, and prevents its function in DNA packaging and cleavage.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations and experimental data.

claim: ORF68 contains three CCCH-type zinc fingers.
source: These residues form three CCCH-type zinc fingers, as supported by the tetrahedral coordination geometry, a large anomalous scattering signal, and C/H composition of the putative zinc fingers, along with the previous observation that the homolog from HSV-1, UL32, binds zinc (Chang et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and a citation to Chang et al., 1996.

claim: The residues that compose the first two zinc fingers of ORF68 (C52, C55, H130, C136 in the first; C296, C299, H366, C373 in the second) are perfectly conserved in all identified homologs.
source: The residues that compose two of these zinc fingers (residues C52, C55, H130, and C136 in the first zinc finger; residues C296, C299, H366, and C373 in the second zinc finger) are perfectly conserved in all identified homologs of ORF68 (Figure 2a, b, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The third zinc finger of ORF68 (C191, C192, C415, H452) is generally conserved in the alpha- and gamma-herpesviruses but is missing in the beta-herpesviruses.
source: The third zinc finger (consisting of C191, C192, C415, and H452) is generally conserved in the alpha- and gamma-herpesviruses (with the exception of the closely related model murine gammaherpesvirus MHV68), but is missing in the beta-herpesviruses (Figure 2c, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The third zinc finger of ORF68 is atypical in that two coordinating residues, C191 and C192, are adjacent to each other.
source: This third zinc finger is also atypical in that two coordinating residues, C191 and C192, are adjacent to each other.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: Noncanonical cysteine organization in a zinc finger has been observed in the structure of RPB10, a subunit of RNA polymerase.
source: Such noncanonical cysteine organization in a zinc finger is rare, but has been observed in the structure of RPB10, a subunit of RNA polymerase (Mackereth et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mackereth et al., 2000.

claim: ORF68 variants with a mutation in any of the zinc fingers were poorly expressed in transfected HEK293T cells.
source: ORF68 variants with a mutation in any of the zinc fingers were poorly expressed in transfected HEK293T cells, suggesting that the zinc fingers are required for structural stability of the protein.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The zinc fingers of ORF68 are required for structural stability of the protein.
source: ORF68 variants with a mutation in any of the zinc fingers were poorly expressed in transfected HEK293T cells, suggesting that the zinc fingers are required for structural stability of the protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that zinc finger mutants are poorly expressed.

claim: Several conserved cysteines in UL32 were previously identified as important for virion production in HSV-1.
source: Several conserved cysteines in UL32 were previously identified as important for virion production in HSV-1 (Albright et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Albright et al., 2015.

claim: The conserved cysteines in UL32 are homologous to the zinc finger residues in ORF68 and are similarly essential for structural stability.
source: We observed that these cysteines in UL32 are homologous to the zinc finger residues in ORF68 and are similarly essential for structural stability as their substitution with alanine resulted in lower UL32 protein levels, whereas mutation of a conserved cysteine outside of the zinc fingers had no effect (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: UL32 likely contains zinc fingers that are required for its structural stability.
source: Thus, UL32 likely also contains zinc fingers that are required for its structural stability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the homology to ORF68 and experimental data.

claim: Wild-type ORF68-expressing cells were able to produce virions sufficient to infect nearly 100% of target cells.
source: Wild-type ORF68-expressing cells were able to produce virions sufficient to infect nearly 100% of target cells, while cells expressing ORF68-C52A were unable to produce progeny virions (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by supernatant transfer assay data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Cells expressing ORF68-C52A were unable to produce progeny virions.
source: Wild-type ORF68-expressing cells were able to produce virions sufficient to infect nearly 100% of target cells, while cells expressing ORF68-C52A were unable to produce progeny virions (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by supernatant transfer assay data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: ORF68-C52A could not be detected by western blot in the context of viral infection.
source: ORF68-C52A could not be detected by western blot, suggesting that the C52A mutation is severely disruptive to the structure of ORF68 even in the context of viral infection (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The C52A mutation is severely disruptive to the structure of ORF68 even in the context of viral infection.
source: ORF68-C52A could not be detected by western blot, suggesting that the C52A mutation is severely disruptive to the structure of ORF68 even in the context of viral infection (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is an inference based on the inability to detect the mutant protein by western blot.

claim: ORF68 homologs can be found in all known members of the Herpesviridae.
source: ORF68 homologs can be found in all known members of the Herpesviridae, although BLAST cannot identify candidates in the Alloherpesviridae and Malacoherpesviridae, distantly related families in the order Herpesvirales that infect fish, amphibians, and mollusks.
evidence: This is based on BLAST searches.

claim: BLAST cannot identify ORF68 homolog candidates in the Alloherpesviridae and Malacoherpesviridae.
source: ORF68 homologs can be found in all known members of the Herpesviridae, although BLAST cannot identify candidates in the Alloherpesviridae and Malacoherpesviridae, distantly related families in the order Herpesvirales that infect fish, amphibians, and mollusks.
evidence: This is based on BLAST searches.

claim: Homologs of ORF68 in the Herpesviridae range in size from 437 residues (MHV68 mu68) to 668 residues (HCMV UL52).
source: Homologs of ORF68 (467 residues) in the Herpesviridae range in size from 437 residues (MHV68 mu68) to 668 residues (HCMV UL52) and show generally low sequence conservation.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: ORF68 homologs show generally low sequence conservation.
source: Homologs of ORF68 (467 residues) in the Herpesviridae range in size from 437 residues (MHV68 mu68) to 668 residues (HCMV UL52) and show generally low sequence conservation.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment.

claim: Conserved residues in ORF68 are generally located in the hydrophobic core, while variable residues map to the surface.
source: Conserved residues in ORF68 are generally located in the hydrophobic core of ORF68, while variable residues map to the surface, particularly the outer faces of the ring (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on conservation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most of the differences in length across ORF68 homologs come from N-terminal extensions or insertions in surface-exposed loops.
source: Most of the differences in length across the homologs come from N-terminal extensions or insertions in surface-exposed loops, suggesting a conserved core structure that is shared across the herpesviruses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: BFLF1 forms decameric rings, consisting of two stacked pentamer rings.
source: Interestingly, size exclusion chromatography and negative stain EM revealed that BFLF1 forms decameric rings, consisting of two stacked pentamer rings (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography and negative stain EM data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a, b.

claim: The structure of BFLF1 was determined by cryo-EM at 3.60 Å resolution.
source: We determined the structure of BFLF1 by cryo-EM at 3.60 Å resolution and found that it forms pentameric rings that are comparable in size to those of ORF68 and with a highly similar structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: BFLF1 forms pentameric rings that are comparable in size to those of ORF68 and with a highly similar structure.
source: We determined the structure of BFLF1 by cryo-EM at 3.60 Å resolution and found that it forms pentameric rings that are comparable in size to those of ORF68 and with a highly similar structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: The BFLF1 structure is highly similar to that of ORF68, with a Root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 1.09 for the monomers and an overall RMSD of 1.95 for the pentameric complexes.
source: The BFLF1 structure is highly similar to that of ORF68, with a Root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 1.09 for the monomers and an overall RMSD of 1.95 for the pentameric complexes (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The internal core of BFLF1, including the first two zinc fingers, is structurally highly conserved compared to ORF68.
source: The internal core of the protein, including the first two zinc fingers (residues C54/C57/H132/C138 and C316/C319/H386/C393 in BFLF1), is structurally highly conserved (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3b.

claim: UL32 formed ring-shaped structures in negative stain EM.
source: We performed negative stain EM on the homolog from HSV-1, UL32, to determine if it also retains homopentameric quaternary structure (Figure 3c). Despite its low overall sequence homology to ORF68 and BFLF1, UL32 formed ring-shaped structures as well, and class averages suggested that it forms a homopentamer.
evidence: This is supported by negative stain EM data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Class averages of UL32 suggested that it forms a homopentamer.
source: We performed negative stain EM on the homolog from HSV-1, UL32, to determine if it also retains homopentameric quaternary structure (Figure 3c). Despite its low overall sequence homology to ORF68 and BFLF1, UL32 formed ring-shaped structures as well, and class averages suggested that it forms a homopentamer.
evidence: This is supported by negative stain EM data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The ability to form a pentameric ring is a common property of ORF68 and its homologs.
source: The ability to form a pentameric ring is therefore a common property of ORF68 and its homologs.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data for ORF68, BFLF1, and UL32.

claim: ORF68.stop cells complemented with ORF68 allowed for production of virions that infected nearly 100% of target cells.
source: As expected, ORF68.stop cells complemented with ORF68 allowed for production of virions that infected nearly 100% of target cells, while complementation with empty vector failed to produce infectious virions.
evidence: This is supported by supernatant transfer assay data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Complementation of ORF68.stop cells with empty vector failed to produce infectious virions.
source: As expected, ORF68.stop cells complemented with ORF68 allowed for production of virions that infected nearly 100% of target cells, while complementation with empty vector failed to produce infectious virions.
evidence: This is supported by supernatant transfer assay data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Homologs from the gamma-herpesviruses, BFLF1 and mu68, were able to partially complement loss of ORF68.
source: Homologs from the gamma-herpesviruses, BFLF1 and mu68, were able to partially complement loss of ORF68, although not to levels comparable to ORF68-expressing cells.
evidence: This is supported by supernatant transfer assay data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Homologs from the alpha- and beta-herpesviruses, UL32 and UL52, failed to complement deletion of ORF68.
source: In contrast, homologs from the more distantly related alpha- and beta-herpesviruses, UL32 and UL52, failed to complement deletion of ORF68.
evidence: This is supported by supernatant transfer assay data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: BFLF1 and mu68 are most similar to ORF68 (35% and 33% identity, respectively).
source: BFLF1 and mu68 are most similar to ORF68 (35% and 33% identity, respectively), while UL32 and UL52 are more diverged in sequence (25% and 22% identity, respectively).
evidence: This is based on sequence identity calculations.

claim: UL32 and UL52 are more diverged in sequence from ORF68 (25% and 22% identity, respectively).
source: BFLF1 and mu68 are most similar to ORF68 (35% and 33% identity, respectively), while UL32 and UL52 are more diverged in sequence (25% and 22% identity, respectively).
evidence: This is based on sequence identity calculations.

claim: Although homologs across the herpesviruses share a common core fold and homopentameric architecture, other features or the identity of surface residues likely play a role in their function and in the interaction with other components during DNA packaging.
source: Thus, although homologs across the herpesviruses share a common core fold and homopentameric architecture, other features or the identity of surface residues likely play a role in their function and in the interaction with other components during DNA packaging.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complementation data and structural observations.

claim: The calculated electrostatic surface of ORF68 shows a striking colocalization of positive charges on one side of the ring around the entrance of the central channel.
source: The calculated electrostatic surface of ORF68 shows a striking colocalization of positive charges on one side of the ring around the entrance of the central channel (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on electrostatic surface calculations shown in Figure 4a.

claim: ORF68 can bind an 800 bp dsDNA probe corresponding to the GC-rich terminal repeat of KSHV.
source: We previously observed that ORF68 can bind an 800 bp dsDNA probe corresponding to the GC-rich terminal repeat of KSHV (Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018), and therefore hypothesized that the electrostatic surface around the central channel of ORF68 could be important for dsDNA binding.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018.

claim: ORF68 binds 10–20 bp dsDNA with high affinity.
source: ORF68 binds 10–20 bp dsDNA with high affinity, while multiple binding events are observed on longer probes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a; Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by electrophoretic mobility shift assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and a citation to Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018.

claim: Multiple binding events are observed when ORF68 binds longer DNA probes.
source: ORF68 binds 10–20 bp dsDNA with high affinity, while multiple binding events are observed on longer probes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a; Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by electrophoretic mobility shift assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and a citation to Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018.

claim: All ORF68 mutants expressed and purified similar to wild-type ORF68.
source: All ORF68 mutants expressed and purified similar to wild-type ORF68 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a), and a representative mutant (ORF68 K435A) behaved similar to wild-type protein in size exclusion chromatography, suggesting that mutations in the central channel do not affect the homopentameric architecture (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: ORF68 K435A behaved similar to wild-type protein in size exclusion chromatography, suggesting that mutations in the central channel do not affect the homopentameric architecture.
source: All ORF68 mutants expressed and purified similar to wild-type ORF68 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a), and a representative mutant (ORF68 K435A) behaved similar to wild-type protein in size exclusion chromatography, suggesting that mutations in the central channel do not affect the homopentameric architecture (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Mutations K435A, R443A, and K174A/R179A/K182A (3+) in ORF68 all resulted in a drastic reduction in DNA binding affinity.
source: Mutations K435A (top, more constricted side of the central channel), R443A (middle of the central channel), and K174A/R179A/K182A (henceforth referred to as '3+', in the disordered region of the central channel) all resulted in a drastic reduction in binding affinity, with negligible interactions even at 4 μM ORF68.
evidence: This is supported by electrophoretic mobility shift assay data shown in Figure 4b, c.

claim: The K450A/R451A mutation in ORF68 bound DNA with lower affinity than wild-type ORF68.
source: The K450A/R451A mutation (bottom of the central channel) bound with lower affinity than wild-type ORF68, as indicated by the lack of concrete bands and a consequential smear.
evidence: This is supported by electrophoretic mobility shift assay data shown in Figure 4b, c.

claim: Mutation in two sets of surface-exposed positive residues located outside the channel, R14A/K310A and K395A/K396A, bound dsDNA comparably to wild-type ORF68 with an effective binding affinity (EC50) of ~25 nM.
source: In contrast, mutation in two sets of surface-exposed positive residues located outside the channel, R14A/K310A and K395A/K396A, bound dsDNA comparably to wild-type ORF68 with an effective binding affinity (EC50) of ~25 nM.
evidence: This is supported by electrophoretic mobility shift assay data shown in Figure 4b, c.

claim: Mutations within the central channel of ORF68 – and specifically near the more constricted top portion – are deleterious to dsDNA binding.
source: Thus, while charge mutations on the periphery of the ring have no effect, mutations within the channel – and specifically near the more constricted top portion – are deleterious to dsDNA binding, likely because residues from all subunits form a large binding interface with high charge density in and near the central channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophoretic mobility shift assay data.

claim: Residues from all subunits of ORF68 form a large binding interface with high charge density in and near the central channel.
source: Thus, while charge mutations on the periphery of the ring have no effect, mutations within the channel – and specifically near the more constricted top portion – are deleterious to dsDNA binding, likely because residues from all subunits form a large binding interface with high charge density in and near the central channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations and binding data.

claim: Herpesviral DNA packaging requires both sequence-specific and nonspecific DNA binding.
source: Herpesviral DNA packaging requires both sequence-specific and nonspecific DNA binding.
evidence: This is established knowledge about herpesviral DNA packaging.

claim: Site-specific binding and cleavage within the terminal repeats is required to ensure full-length genomes are packaged.
source: Site-specific binding and cleavage within the terminal repeats is required to ensure full-length genomes are packaged; however, this role is thought to be fulfilled by the terminase (Adelman et al., 2001; Theiß et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Adelman et al., 2001 and Theiß et al., 2019.

claim: The role of site-specific binding and cleavage within the terminal repeats is thought to be fulfilled by the terminase.
source: Site-specific binding and cleavage within the terminal repeats is required to ensure full-length genomes are packaged; however, this role is thought to be fulfilled by the terminase (Adelman et al., 2001; Theiß et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Adelman et al., 2001 and Theiß et al., 2019.

claim: HSV-1 UL25 (KSHV ORF19) binds DNA and has recently been shown to be the 'portal cap' that prevents DNA escape after packaging has been completed.
source: Packaging also depends on nonsequence-specific interactions with various factors, such as HSV-1 UL25 (KSHV ORF19) that binds DNA and has recently been shown to be the 'portal cap' that prevents DNA escape after packaging has been completed (Gong et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Ogasawara et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019; and Ogasawara et al., 2001.

claim: ORF68 bound with ~25 nM affinity to both a GC-rich sequence and a scrambled sequence with 50% GC content.
source: ORF68 bound with ~25 nM affinity to both substrates, suggesting that it recognizes dsDNA in vitro in a nonsequence-specific manner.
evidence: This is supported by electrophoretic mobility shift assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: ORF68 recognizes dsDNA in vitro in a nonsequence-specific manner.
source: ORF68 bound with ~25 nM affinity to both substrates, suggesting that it recognizes dsDNA in vitro in a nonsequence-specific manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ORF68 binds GC-rich and scrambled sequences with similar affinity.

claim: The ORF68-K435A cell line had a pronounced virion-production defect, leading to infection of <5% of target cells.
source: The ORF68-K435A cells had a pronounced virion-production defect, leading to infection of <5% of target cells, and the ORF68-3+ cell line failed to produce any infectious virions.
evidence: This is supported by supernatant transfer assay data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The ORF68-3+ cell line failed to produce any infectious virions.
source: The ORF68-K435A cells had a pronounced virion-production defect, leading to infection of <5% of target cells, and the ORF68-3+ cell line failed to produce any infectious virions.
evidence: This is supported by supernatant transfer assay data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Both the ORF68-K435A and 3+ mutant rescue (MR) cell lines behaved similar to wild-type KSHV-infected cells.
source: Both the ORF68-K435A and 3+ MR cell lines behaved similar to wild-type KSHV-infected cells, confirming that defects in virion production are caused by the charge mutations in ORF68, rather than effects on neighboring genes or mutations elsewhere in the viral genome acquired during recombination.
evidence: This is supported by supernatant transfer assay data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Defects in virion production in the K435A and 3+ mutants are caused by the charge mutations in ORF68, rather than effects on neighboring genes or mutations elsewhere in the viral genome acquired during recombination.
source: Both the ORF68-K435A and 3+ MR cell lines behaved similar to wild-type KSHV-infected cells, confirming that defects in virion production are caused by the charge mutations in ORF68, rather than effects on neighboring genes or mutations elsewhere in the viral genome acquired during recombination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue of the phenotype by reversion of the mutations.

claim: The K435A and 3+ mutations retain wild-type levels of ORF68 expression.
source: Importantly, the K435A and 3+ mutations retain wild-type levels of ORF68 expression (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: A small but consistent reduction in the expression level of the late gene K8.1 can be observed in the ORF68.stop, ORF68-K435A, and ORF68-3+ cell lines.
source: Interestingly, a small but consistent reduction in the expression level of the late gene K8.1 can be observed in the ORF68.stop, ORF68-K435A, and ORF68-3+ cell lines, suggesting that ORF68 may have other minor roles in gene expression or protein homeostasis during infection.
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: ORF68 may have other minor roles in gene expression or protein homeostasis during infection.
source: Interestingly, a small but consistent reduction in the expression level of the late gene K8.1 can be observed in the ORF68.stop, ORF68-K435A, and ORF68-3+ cell lines, suggesting that ORF68 may have other minor roles in gene expression or protein homeostasis during infection.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of reduced K8.1 expression.

claim: There was no difference in viral DNA replication between the wild-type virus and the ORF68.stop, ORF68-K435A, or ORF68-3+ viruses.
source: We measured viral DNA replication by qPCR and found no difference between the wild-type virus and the ORF68.stop, ORF68-K435A, or ORF68-3+ viruses (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The ORF68-K435A and 3+ cell lines reveal prominent defects in genome cleavage.
source: Similar to cells lacking ORF68, the ORF68-K435A and 3+ cell lines reveal prominent defects in genome cleavage that are rescued by their respective MR lines (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The virion production defect observed in the K435A and 3+ cell lines is caused by a failure to properly cleave and package the viral genome.
source: Thus, the virion production defect observed in the K435A and 3+ cell lines is caused by a failure to properly cleave and package the viral genome, suggesting that the ability of ORF68 to bind nucleic acid through its positively charged central channel is required for successful packaging.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Southern blot data showing cleavage defects.

claim: The ability of ORF68 to bind nucleic acid through its positively charged central channel is required for successful packaging.
source: Thus, the virion production defect observed in the K435A and 3+ cell lines is caused by a failure to properly cleave and package the viral genome, suggesting that the ability of ORF68 to bind nucleic acid through its positively charged central channel is required for successful packaging.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data showing that channel mutants lose DNA binding and fail to package genomes.

claim: ORF68 adopts a novel homopentameric ring structure with largely α-helical monomers stabilized by multiple zinc fingers.
source: Here, we present the structure of the only functionally undefined component of the herpesviral packaging machinery and reveal that its ability to bind DNA, likely involving its positively charged central channel, is critical for genome packaging. KSHV ORF68 adopts a novel homopentameric ring structure with largely α-helical monomers stabilized by multiple zinc fingers.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM.

claim: Comparison to the EBV BFLF1 structure reveals extremely high structural homology.
source: Comparison to the EBV BFLF1 structure reveals extremely high structural homology, and negative stain EM analyses of a homolog from a further diverged alphaherpesvirus suggest a common monomer fold and potential to form pentameric quaternary structure.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and negative stain EM data.

claim: Negative stain EM analyses of UL32 suggest a common monomer fold and potential to form pentameric quaternary structure.
source: Comparison to the EBV BFLF1 structure reveals extremely high structural homology, and negative stain EM analyses of a homolog from a further diverged alphaherpesvirus suggest a common monomer fold and potential to form pentameric quaternary structure.
evidence: This is supported by negative stain EM data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: It is likely that the core architecture of ORF68 homologs is conserved across herpesviruses from all subfamilies.
source: Thus, it is likely that the core architecture is conserved across herpesviruses from all subfamilies.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data for ORF68, BFLF1, and UL32.

claim: The importance of ORF68 and its homologs for genome cleavage and packaging has been studied in several herpesviruses, and deletion of these proteins results in a common phenotype, indicative of a conserved function.
source: The importance of ORF68 and its homologs for genome cleavage and packaging has been studied in several herpesviruses, and deletion of these proteins results in a common phenotype, indicative of a conserved function (Albright et al., 2015; Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018; Lamberti and Weller, 1998; Borst et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Albright et al., 2015; Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018; Lamberti and Weller, 1998; and Borst et al., 2008.

claim: UL32 has been described as a glycoprotein.
source: UL32, the homolog from HSV-1, has been described as a glycoprotein (Becker et al., 1988), yet functional and structural analyses by us and others suggest that this is not the case (Chang et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Becker et al., 1988.

claim: Functional and structural analyses suggest that UL32 is not a glycoprotein.
source: UL32, the homolog from HSV-1, has been described as a glycoprotein (Becker et al., 1988), yet functional and structural analyses by us and others suggest that this is not the case (Chang et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chang et al., 1996 and the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Studies in HSV-1 and HCMV demonstrate that the homologs of ORF68 are not involved in expression or localization of the portal or terminase.
source: Studies in HSV-1 and HCMV demonstrate that the homologs of ORF68 are not involved in expression or localization of the portal or terminase as deletion of UL32 or UL52, respectively, has no effect on these properties (Borst et al., 2008; Yu and Weller, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borst et al., 2008 and Yu and Weller, 1998.

claim: Deletion of UL32 or UL52 has no effect on expression or localization of the portal or terminase.
source: Studies in HSV-1 and HCMV demonstrate that the homologs of ORF68 are not involved in expression or localization of the portal or terminase as deletion of UL32 or UL52, respectively, has no effect on these properties (Borst et al., 2008; Yu and Weller, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borst et al., 2008 and Yu and Weller, 1998.

claim: Mass spectrometry data from different purified herpesviruses and recent cryo-EM reconstructions of herpesvirus capsids suggest that neither ORF68 nor its homologs are stably capsid-associated or packaged into virions.
source: A plethora of mass spectrometry data from different purified herpesviruses, along with recent cryo-EM reconstructions of herpesvirus capsids, suggest that neither ORF68 nor its homologs are stably capsid-associated or packaged into virions.
evidence: This is based on a review of mass spectrometry and cryo-EM data from the literature.

claim: Similarities between the capsid structure, portal, and terminase in tailed bacteriophages and herpesviruses strongly suggest that these viruses share ancestrally ancient packaging machinery.
source: Similarities between the capsid structure, portal, and terminase in tailed bacteriophages and herpesviruses strongly suggest that these viruses share ancestrally ancient packaging machinery (McGeoch et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McGeoch et al., 2006.

claim: ORF68 has no identifiable structural or functional homolog in phages.
source: Although ORF68 has no identifiable structural or functional homolog in phages, several previously studied model phages have accessory factors critical for efficient packaging.
evidence: This is based on structural and sequence comparisons.

claim: Several previously studied model phages have accessory factors critical for efficient packaging.
source: Although ORF68 has no identifiable structural or functional homolog in phages, several previously studied model phages have accessory factors critical for efficient packaging.
evidence: This is established knowledge about phage packaging.

claim: In phage λ, the factor gpFI is required for efficient packaging.
source: In phage λ, the factor gpFI is required for efficient packaging (Becker et al., 1988; Davidson and Gold, 1987; Sippy and Feiss, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Becker et al., 1988; Davidson and Gold, 1987; and Sippy and Feiss, 2004.

claim: gpFI is thought to facilitate binding of the DNA-engaged terminase to the capsid (prohead) through interactions with the major head protein.
source: gpFI is thought to facilitate binding of the DNA-engaged terminase to the capsid (prohead) through interactions with the major head protein (Becker et al., 1988; Davidson and Gold, 1987; Popovic et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Becker et al., 1988; Davidson and Gold, 1987; and Popovic et al., 2012.

claim: Phage phi29 encodes a pentameric structural RNA (pRNA) that is sandwiched between the portal and terminase during packaging.
source: Phage phi29 encodes a pentameric structural RNA (pRNA) that is sandwiched between the portal and terminase during packaging (Ding et al., 2011; Simpson et al., 2000; Woodson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ding et al., 2011; Simpson et al., 2000; and Woodson et al., 2020.

claim: ORF68 may act as a bridge between the portal and the terminase, by analogy to phage accessory factors.
source: Although structurally unrelated to gpFI or pRNA, ORF68 by analogy may act as a bridge between the portal and the terminase.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to phage systems.

claim: Recent reconstructions of the HSV-1 and KSHV capsids revealed their structures at atomic resolution and resolved the portal vertex through which the DNA genome is packaged.
source: Recent reconstructions of the HSV-1 and KSHV capsids (Gong et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019) revealed their structures at atomic resolution and resolved the portal vertex through which the DNA genome is packaged.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2019 and Liu et al., 2019.

claim: The portal cap, which has pentameric symmetry, sits atop the portal vertex and is thought to be composed of HSV-1 UL25 (KSHV ORF19).
source: The portal cap, which has pentameric symmetry, sits atop this vertex and is thought to be composed of HSV-1 UL25 (KSHV ORF19).
evidence: This is based on recent structural studies.

claim: Binding of the portal cap to the portal vertex reveals how proteins with pentameric symmetry, like ORF68, could interface with the dodecameric portal.
source: Notably, binding of the portal cap to the portal vertex reveals how proteins with pentameric symmetry, like ORF68, could interface with the dodecameric portal.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: ORF68's role in packaging is to assist docking of the DNA-bound terminase complex with the portal machinery, perhaps by acting as a scaffold that confers fivefold symmetry for the terminase.
source: We propose that ORF68's role in packaging is to assist docking of the DNA-bound terminase complex with the portal machinery, perhaps by acting as a scaffold that confers fivefold symmetry for the terminase (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural and functional data presented.

claim: Nonspecific DNA binding by ORF68 could promote formation of the terminase–DNA complex and drive the packaging reaction forward.
source: Nonspecific DNA binding by ORF68 could promote formation of the terminase–DNA complex and drive the packaging reaction forward.
evidence: This is speculation based on the DNA binding properties of ORF68.

claim: The genome may thread through the channel of the pentameric ORF68 ring.
source: The genome may thread through the channel of the pentameric ring, which in its most constricted region is just wide enough to accommodate dsDNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is speculation based on the dimensions of the central channel shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A recent structure of the terminase complex from HSV-1 revealed hexameric symmetry in solution.
source: Although a recent structure of the terminase complex from HSV-1 revealed hexameric symmetry in solution, its symmetry while bound to the portal remains unknown (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2020.

claim: The symmetry of the HSV-1 terminase complex while bound to the portal remains unknown.
source: Although a recent structure of the terminase complex from HSV-1 revealed hexameric symmetry in solution, its symmetry while bound to the portal remains unknown (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Phage motors can adopt different stoichiometries, but actively packaging motors are thought to be pentameric.
source: It is well established that phage motors can adopt different stoichiometries, but actively packaging motors are thought to be pentameric (Woodson et al., 2020; Hilbert et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Woodson et al., 2020; Hilbert et al., 2015; and Sun et al., 2008.

claim: ORF68 could be involved in the initial generation of a free dsDNA end for packaging.
source: Alternatively, ORF68 could be involved in the initial generation of a free dsDNA end for packaging, a process which is poorly understood.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative role for ORF68.

claim: Herpesvirus genome replication produces branched, head-to-tail concatemers that are cleaved within a repeated region during packaging to produce a packaged capsid containing a unit-length genome.
source: Herpesvirus genome replication produces branched, head-to-tail concatemers that are cleaved within a repeated region (the terminal repeats in KSHV [Lagunoff and Ganem, 1997]; the directly repeated element [DR1] within the a sequence at the UL terminus in HSV-1) during packaging to produce a packaged capsid containing a unit-length genome (reviewed in Heming et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lagunoff and Ganem, 1997 and Heming et al., 2017.

claim: An initial cleavage event to produce a substrate for packaging must occur since replication of the viral genome does not initiate within the repeated regions.
source: Since replication of the viral genome does not initiate within these repeated regions, an initial cleavage event to produce a substrate for packaging must occur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of herpesvirus genome replication.

claim: Of the seven herpesviral genes required for successful packaging, when deleted, all except UL25 have the additional effect of preventing cleavage.
source: Of the seven herpesviral genes required for successful packaging (HSV-1 UL6, UL15, UL17, UL25, UL28, UL32, and UL33), when deleted, all of these except UL25 have the additional effect of preventing cleavage, which is closely tied to packaging.
evidence: This is established knowledge about herpesviral packaging genes.

claim: ORF68 and its homologs may be involved in either the preparation of the initial substrate for packaging (generation of the initial cut) or regulation of the cleavage event during subsequent rounds of packaging.
source: ORF68 and its homologs may thus be involved in either the preparation of the initial substrate for packaging (generation of the initial cut) (Figure 6b) or regulation of the cleavage event during subsequent rounds of packaging.
evidence: This is speculation about possible roles for ORF68.

claim: Coupling between packaging, DNA replication, and late gene machinery has been observed in phage.
source: An additional possibility could include a role for ORF68 and its homologs in the coordination of packaging with DNA replication and late gene machinery, as coupling between these processes has been observed in phage (Black and Peng, 2006), and several capsid components have been shown to interact with replicating viral genomes in HSV-1 (Dembowski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Black and Peng, 2006 and Dembowski et al., 2017.

claim: Several capsid components have been shown to interact with replicating viral genomes in HSV-1.
source: An additional possibility could include a role for ORF68 and its homologs in the coordination of packaging with DNA replication and late gene machinery, as coupling between these processes has been observed in phage (Black and Peng, 2006), and several capsid components have been shown to interact with replicating viral genomes in HSV-1 (Dembowski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dembowski et al., 2017.

claim: Although ORF68 and its homologs share a conserved structure and likely play similar roles in packaging across the herpesviruses, they are expressed with divergent kinetics, suggesting potential additional functions.
source: Although ORF68 and its homologs share a conserved structure and likely play similar roles in packaging across the herpesviruses, they are expressed with divergent kinetics, suggesting potential additional functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of divergent expression kinetics.

claim: HSV-1 UL32 and HCMV UL52 are late genes, consistent with a primary role in packaging.
source: HSV-1 UL32 and HCMV UL52 are late genes, consistent with a primary role in packaging (Albright et al., 2015; Borst et al., 2008), whereas KSHV ORF68 is an early gene, accumulating prior to the expression of several capsid proteins (Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Albright et al., 2015; Borst et al., 2008; and Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018.

claim: KSHV ORF68 is an early gene, accumulating prior to the expression of several capsid proteins.
source: HSV-1 UL32 and HCMV UL52 are late genes, consistent with a primary role in packaging (Albright et al., 2015; Borst et al., 2008), whereas KSHV ORF68 is an early gene, accumulating prior to the expression of several capsid proteins (Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gardner and Glaunsinger, 2018.

claim: It remains to be determined whether ORF68 has additional roles early in infection.
source: It remains to be determined whether ORF68 has additional roles early in infection.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge and future research directions.

claim: Deletion of ORF68 can be partially complemented by other gammaherpesvirus homologs (mu68 and BFLF1).
source: We demonstrated that deletion of ORF68 can be partially complemented by other gammaherpesvirus homologs (mu68 and BFLF1).
evidence: This is supported by complementation assay data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Deletion of the ORF68 homolog in the alphaherpesvirus pseudorabies virus (PrV) can be partially complemented by expression of HSV-1 UL32.
source: Interestingly, deletion of the ORF68 homolog in the alphaherpesvirus pseudorabies virus (PrV) can be partially complemented by expression of HSV-1 UL32; however, the inverse complementation was not observed, indicating that some functions or interactions are sufficiently similar for PrV virion production but not HSV-1 virion production (Fuchs et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fuchs et al., 2009.

claim: The inverse complementation (HSV-1 deletion complemented by PrV homolog) was not observed.
source: Interestingly, deletion of the ORF68 homolog in the alphaherpesvirus pseudorabies virus (PrV) can be partially complemented by expression of HSV-1 UL32; however, the inverse complementation was not observed, indicating that some functions or interactions are sufficiently similar for PrV virion production but not HSV-1 virion production (Fuchs et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fuchs et al., 2009.

claim: Some functions or interactions of ORF68 homologs are sufficiently similar for PrV virion production but not HSV-1 virion production.
source: Interestingly, deletion of the ORF68 homolog in the alphaherpesvirus pseudorabies virus (PrV) can be partially complemented by expression of HSV-1 UL32; however, the inverse complementation was not observed, indicating that some functions or interactions are sufficiently similar for PrV virion production but not HSV-1 virion production (Fuchs et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the complementation data cited from Fuchs et al., 2009.

claim: PrV UL32 and HSV-1 UL32 share ~52% sequence similarity, as do ORF68 and EBV BFLF1 or MHV mu68.
source: PrV UL32 and HSV-1 UL32 share ~52% sequence similarity, as do ORF68 and EBV BFLF1 or MHV mu68, suggesting that in both cases common residues or structural motifs mediate shared interactions to carry out critical functions in the cell.
evidence: This is based on sequence similarity calculations.

claim: Common residues or structural motifs mediate shared interactions to carry out critical functions in the cell.
source: PrV UL32 and HSV-1 UL32 share ~52% sequence similarity, as do ORF68 and EBV BFLF1 or MHV mu68, suggesting that in both cases common residues or structural motifs mediate shared interactions to carry out critical functions in the cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequence similarity and complementation data.

claim: There is no cure for any herpesvirus.
source: Despite widespread prevalence of herpesviruses and the significant diseases they cause, there is no cure for any herpesvirus, and a vaccine exists only for the alpha-herpesvirus varicella zoster virus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about herpesvirus therapeutics.

claim: A vaccine exists only for the alpha-herpesvirus varicella zoster virus.
source: Despite widespread prevalence of herpesviruses and the significant diseases they cause, there is no cure for any herpesvirus, and a vaccine exists only for the alpha-herpesvirus varicella zoster virus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about herpesvirus vaccines.

claim: The majority of antiherpesviral drugs target the DNA replication machinery.
source: The majority of antiherpesviral drugs target the DNA replication machinery, but have several disadvantages, including the emergence of resistance mutations and a narrow spectrum of use (Coen and Schaffer, 2003; Poole and James, 2018; Weller and Kuchta, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coen and Schaffer, 2003; Poole and James, 2018; and Weller and Kuchta, 2013.

claim: Antiherpesviral drugs targeting DNA replication machinery have several disadvantages, including the emergence of resistance mutations and a narrow spectrum of use.
source: The majority of antiherpesviral drugs target the DNA replication machinery, but have several disadvantages, including the emergence of resistance mutations and a narrow spectrum of use (Coen and Schaffer, 2003; Poole and James, 2018; Weller and Kuchta, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coen and Schaffer, 2003; Poole and James, 2018; and Weller and Kuchta, 2013.

claim: Letermovir is a drug recently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of HCMV in stem cell transplant recipients.
source: However, Letermovir, a drug recently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of HCMV in stem cell transplant recipients, targets the HCMV terminase through an unknown mechanism (Goldner et al., 2011; Ligat et al., 2018; Lischka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goldner et al., 2011; Ligat et al., 2018; and Lischka et al., 2010.

claim: Letermovir targets the HCMV terminase through an unknown mechanism.
source: However, Letermovir, a drug recently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of HCMV in stem cell transplant recipients, targets the HCMV terminase through an unknown mechanism (Goldner et al., 2011; Ligat et al., 2018; Lischka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goldner et al., 2011; Ligat et al., 2018; and Lischka et al., 2010.

claim: Letermovir lacks activity against other herpesviruses.
source: Letermovir lacks activity against other herpesviruses (Marschall et al., 2012), suggesting that key differences exist in their conserved machinery.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marschall et al., 2012.

claim: Key differences exist in the conserved packaging machinery of different herpesviruses.
source: Letermovir lacks activity against other herpesviruses (Marschall et al., 2012), suggesting that key differences exist in their conserved machinery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Letermovir is specific to HCMV.

claim: Understanding the molecular underpinnings of packaging and the differences in mechanism across the alpha-, beta-, and gamma-herpesviruses is critical for the future development of antiherpesvirals as effective therapeutics.
source: Understanding the molecular underpinnings of packaging and the differences in mechanism across the alpha-, beta-, and gamma-herpesviruses is critical for the future development of antiherpesvirals as effective therapeutics.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of the research for future drug development.
